label: Apology · The Defense
title: The Defense
paragraphs: What effect my accusers have had on you, men of Athens, I do not know. As for me, they almost made me forget who I am, they spoke so persuasively. And yet hardly a word of what they said is true. Of their many lies, one amazed me most: they told you to be on your guard against being deceived by me, because I am a clever speaker. They were not ashamed to say it, though I am about to refute them at once by the plain fact, as soon as it appears that I am no clever speaker at all; and that seemed to me the most shameless thing about them — unless, of course, they call a man a clever speaker who tells the truth. If that is what they mean, I would agree that I am an orator, though not one of their kind. These men, as I say, have said little or nothing that is true. From me you will hear the whole truth — but not, by Zeus, men of Athens, in speeches like theirs, dressed up in fine words and phrases and carefully arranged. You will hear things said as they come, in the first words that occur to me, for I trust that what I say is just; and let none of you expect anything else. It would hardly be fitting, gentlemen, for a man of my age to come before you shaping speeches like a schoolboy. And I do ask this of you, men of Athens, and beg it: if you hear me making my defense in the same words I am used to speaking in the marketplace by the bankers' tables, where many of you have heard me, and elsewhere, do not be surprised and do not make an uproar over it. The fact is this. I am seventy years old, and this is the first time I have ever come before a court; so I am simply a stranger to the way of speaking here. If I really were a foreigner, you would surely forgive me for speaking in the dialect and the manner I was brought up in. So now I make this request of you, and I think it a just one: never mind my manner of speaking — it may be worse, it may be better — and look only at this, and give your mind to this: whether what I say is just or not. For that is the excellence of a judge, as an orator's is to tell the truth.

First, then, men of Athens, it is right that I answer the first false charges against me and my first accusers, and then the later charges and the later accusers. For many have accused me before you, and for many years now, and nothing they said was true; and I am more afraid of them than of Anytus and his friends, though these are dangerous too. But those others are more dangerous, gentlemen. They got hold of most of you as children, and persuaded you, and accused me with no truth in it at all: There is a man called Socrates, a wise man, a thinker about the things in the sky, who has searched out everything under the earth, and who makes the weaker argument the stronger. Those men, men of Athens, who have spread this report about me, are my dangerous accusers; for the people who hear them suppose that anyone who inquires into such things does not believe in the gods either. Then too, these accusers are many, and they have been accusing me a long time; and besides, they spoke to you at the age when you were most likely to believe them, when some of you were children and some were youths, and they were accusing me simply by default, with no one there to make a defense. And the most unreasonable thing of all is that I cannot even know their names and tell you them — unless one of them happens to be a writer of comedies. All those who won you over out of envy and slander, and those who, once persuaded themselves, went on to persuade others — all of these are the hardest to deal with. I cannot bring a single one of them up here to question him. I must simply fight with shadows in making my defense, and cross-examine with no one to answer. So accept, as I say, that my accusers are of two kinds: those who have accused me just now, and the old ones I am speaking of. And agree that I must answer the old ones first; for you heard them accusing me first, and heard far more from them than from these later ones.

Well then. I must make my defense, men of Athens, and try to take out of your minds, in so short a time, a slander you have been so long in acquiring. I would wish it to turn out so, if that is better for you and for me, and I would wish my defense to succeed. But I think it is hard, and I am not at all blind to what kind of task it is. Still, let this go as the god pleases. The law must be obeyed, and I must make my defense.

Let us take it up from the beginning, then. What is the accusation from which the slander against me arose — the slander Meletus trusted in when he brought this charge against me? Well, what did the slanderers say when they slandered me? I must read out their sworn statement, as if they were my accusers in court: ‘Socrates does wrong and meddles, inquiring into things under the earth and in the sky, making the weaker argument the stronger, and teaching others to do the same.’ It runs something like that. You saw it yourselves in the comedy of Aristophanes: a Socrates swinging around up there, declaring that he walks on air and talking a great deal of other nonsense about things of which I understand nothing, great or small. And I do not say this in contempt of such knowledge, if anyone is wise in these matters — I would not want Meletus bringing me to trial on a charge as heavy as that! But the truth is, men of Athens, I have no part in these things. I offer most of you as my witnesses, and I ask you to inform one another and speak up, all of you who have ever heard me in conversation — and there are many such among you. Tell one another, then, whether any of you has ever heard me discussing such things, in few words or many. From that you will see that the other things people say about me are of the same kind.

No, there is nothing in any of it. And if you have heard from anyone that I undertake to educate people and charge a fee for it, that is not true either. Though I do think it a fine thing, if a man were able to educate people, as Gorgias of Leontini does, and Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis. Each of these men, gentlemen, can go into any city and persuade the young — who may keep company for nothing with any of their own fellow citizens they choose — to leave that company, to keep company with him instead, to pay money for it, and to be grateful besides. For that matter, there is another wise man here, from Paros, who I learned was in town. I happened to meet a man who has paid more money to sophists than everyone else put together, Callias the son of Hipponicus. So I asked him — he has two sons — Callias, I said, if your two sons had been colts or calves, we would be able to find and hire someone to look after them, who would make them fine and good in the virtue proper to them; and he would be some horse trainer or farmer. But as it is, since they are human beings, whom do you have in mind to look after them? Who has knowledge of that kind of virtue, the virtue of a human being and a citizen? I suppose you have looked into it, having sons. Is there anyone, I said, or not? Certainly, he said. Who? I said. Where is he from, and what does he charge to teach? Evenus, Socrates, he said, from Paros; five minas. And I thought Evenus a fortunate man, if he really has this skill and teaches for so moderate a fee. I myself would certainly preen and give myself airs if I knew these things. But I do not know them, men of Athens.

Perhaps one of you might reply: But Socrates, what is it that you do? Where have these slanders against you come from? Surely all this talk and rumor did not arise while you were busy with nothing more unusual than other people, unless you were doing something different from what most people do. So tell us what it is, so that we do not judge your case offhand. Anyone who says this seems to me to speak justly, and I will try to show you what it is that has brought me this name and this slander. Listen, then. Perhaps some of you will think I am joking; but be sure of it, I will tell you the whole truth. I have gained this name, men of Athens, through nothing but a certain wisdom. What kind of wisdom? The kind that is perhaps human wisdom. In that, it may be, I really am wise. The men I spoke of just now may be wise with some wisdom greater than human, or else I do not know what to say of it; for I certainly do not have it, and whoever says I do is lying and speaks to slander me. And, men of Athens, do not make an uproar, even if I seem to you to be boasting. The words I am going to speak are not mine; I will refer you to a speaker who deserves your trust. Of my wisdom — if it is wisdom at all — and of what kind it is, I will offer you as witness the god at Delphi. You knew Chaerephon, I think. He was my friend from our youth, and a friend of your popular party; he went into exile with you in the recent exile, and came back with you. And you know what Chaerephon was like, how intense he was in whatever he set out to do. Well, he once went to Delphi and dared to put this question to the oracle — and as I say, gentlemen, do not make an uproar — he asked whether anyone was wiser than I. And the Pythian priestess answered that no one was wiser. His brother here will testify to you about this, since Chaerephon himself is dead.

Now consider why I tell you this: I am going to show you where the slander against me came from. When I heard the answer, I thought it over like this: What can the god mean? What is his riddle? For I am aware that I am not wise in anything, great or small. What then can he mean by saying that I am the wisest? He is surely not lying; that is not permitted to him. For a long time I was at a loss what he meant. Then, very reluctantly, I turned to inquire into it in the following way. I went to one of those with a reputation for wisdom, thinking that there, if anywhere, I would refute the oracle and show the god: This man here is wiser than I am, and you said I was the wisest. So I examined him — I need not give his name; he was one of the politicians — and when I examined him and talked with him, men of Athens, this is what happened to me. It seemed to me that this man seemed wise to many other people, and above all to himself, but was not. And then I tried to show him that he thought he was wise but was not. As a result I came to be hated by him and by many of those present. But as I went away I reasoned with myself: I am wiser than this man. Probably neither of us knows anything fine and good; but he thinks he knows something when he does not, while I, just as I do not know, do not think I know either. So I seem to be wiser than he is by just this little: what I do not know, I do not think I know. After that I went to another man, one of those thought wiser than the first, and it seemed to me exactly the same; and there too I came to be hated, by him and by many others.

After that I went on from one to the next. I saw, with pain and with fear, that I was coming to be hated; but all the same it seemed necessary to put the god's business first. So I had to go on, looking into what the oracle meant, to everyone with a reputation for knowing something. And by the dog, men of Athens — for I must tell you the truth — this, I swear, is what happened to me. Those with the highest reputations seemed to me, as I searched in the god's service, to be very nearly the most lacking, while others who were thought their inferiors were men of better sense. I must describe my wanderings to you, then, as a kind of labors that I labored, all so that the oracle might stand unrefuted. After the politicians I went to the poets, the writers of tragedies and of dithyrambs and the rest, sure that there I would catch myself in the act, more ignorant than they were. So I took up the poems on which I thought they had worked the hardest, and questioned them closely about what they meant, hoping at the same time to learn something from them. I am ashamed to tell you the truth, gentlemen, but it must be told. Almost anyone standing by, one might say, could have spoken better than the poets about the poems they themselves had made. So I soon saw this about the poets too: they did not make what they made by wisdom, but by some gift of nature, and under inspiration, like the seers and the givers of oracles. For these too say many fine things and know nothing of what they say. Something like that, it appeared to me, was the case with the poets as well. And I noticed at the same time that, because of their poetry, they thought themselves the wisest of men in other things too, in which they were not. So I left them as well, thinking I had the same advantage over them that I had over the politicians.

Last of all I went to the craftsmen. For I was aware that I knew practically nothing, and I was sure I would find that they knew many fine things. And in that I was not mistaken: they did know things I did not know, and in that way they were wiser than I. But, men of Athens, the good craftsmen seemed to me to have the same fault as the poets. Because he practiced his own craft well, each one thought himself very wise in the other, most important matters too; and this false note of theirs drowned out the wisdom they had. So I asked myself, on the oracle's behalf, whether I would choose to be as I am, neither wise with their wisdom nor ignorant with their ignorance, or to have both, as they do. And I answered myself and the oracle that I am better off as I am.

From this examination, men of Athens, much hatred has come upon me, of the harshest and heaviest kind, and from the hatred many slanders; and from it comes this name of being wise. For on each occasion the bystanders think that I myself am wise in the matters where I refute someone else. But the truth probably is, gentlemen, that the god is the one who is really wise, and in this oracle he is saying that human wisdom is worth little or nothing. And he appears to speak of this man Socrates, and to use my name, only to make an example of me, as if he were to say: The wisest of you, human beings, is the one who, like Socrates, has recognized that in truth he is worth nothing where wisdom is concerned. That is why, even now, I still go about searching and inquiring, as the god would have me, among citizens and strangers alike, whenever I think one of them is wise. And when he seems to me not to be, I come to the god's aid and show him that he is not wise. And because of this occupation I have had no leisure to do anything worth mentioning in the city's affairs or in my own. I live in great poverty because of my service to the god.

And besides this, the young men who follow me around of their own accord — the ones with the most leisure, the sons of the richest families — enjoy hearing people examined, and they often imitate me themselves and try their hand at examining others. And then, I suppose, they find no shortage of people who think they know something and know little or nothing. As a result, the people they examine are angry with me, not with themselves, and say that there is one Socrates, a thoroughly foul man, who corrupts the young. And when anyone asks them what he does and what he teaches to corrupt them, they have nothing to say; they do not know. But so as not to seem at a loss, they say the things that are always ready to hand against everyone who pursues philosophy: ‘the things in the sky and under the earth,’ and ‘not believing in gods,’ and ‘making the weaker argument the stronger.’ The truth, I imagine, they would not care to tell: that they have been shown up as pretending to know when they know nothing. So, since they are ambitious, I think, and forceful, and many, and since they speak of me earnestly and persuasively, they have filled your ears with their violent slander, for a long time now. On the strength of this, Meletus attacked me, and Anytus, and Lycon — Meletus aggrieved on behalf of the poets, Anytus on behalf of the craftsmen and the politicians, and Lycon on behalf of the orators. So that, as I said at the beginning, I would be surprised if I were able to take this slander out of your minds in so short a time, when it has grown so great. There, men of Athens, you have the truth. I speak without hiding anything from you, great or small, and without holding anything back. And yet I am fairly sure that it is for these very things that I am hated — which is itself a proof that I am telling the truth, and that this is the slander against me, and these are its causes. Whether you look into it now or later, that is what you will find.

So much, then, for my defense before you against the charges of my first accusers. Next I will try to defend myself against Meletus, that good man and lover of his city, as he says, and the later accusers. Once again, since these are a different set of accusers, let us take up their sworn statement in turn. It runs something like this. It says that Socrates does wrong by corrupting the young, and by not believing in the gods the city believes in, but in other, new divine things. Such is the charge. Let us examine each point of it, one by one.

He says that I do wrong by corrupting the young. But I say, men of Athens, that Meletus does wrong, because he makes a joke of a serious matter: he lightly brings people to trial, pretending to be earnest and to care about things to which he has never given a thought. That this is so I will try to show you too.
Come here, Meletus, and tell me: don't you think it of the greatest importance that the young should be as good as possible?
I do.

Come then, tell these men who makes them better. Clearly you know, since you care so much. You have found the one who corrupts them, as you say — me — and you bring me before these men and accuse me. So come, tell them who makes the young better; point him out to them. You see, Meletus? You are silent, and have nothing to say. Doesn't that seem shameful to you, and proof enough of what I say, that you have never cared? But tell us, my good man, who makes them better?
The laws.
That's not what I am asking, my good friend. What person — who must know that very thing, the laws, to begin with?
These men, Socrates, the judges.
What do you mean, Meletus? These men are able to educate the young, and make them better?
Certainly.
All of them? Or some of them and not others?
All of them.
By Hera, that is good news — no shortage of benefactors. And what about the audience here? Do they make the young better or not?
They do too.
And the members of the Council?
The members of the Council too.
But surely, Meletus, the men in the Assembly, the Assembly members, don't corrupt the young? Or do they all make them better as well?
They do as well.
So every Athenian, it seems, makes them fine and good, except me, and I alone corrupt them. Is that what you are saying?
That is exactly what I am saying.

You have condemned me to great misfortune. Now answer me this: do you think it is the same with horses? Are those who make them better all of mankind, while one man corrupts them? Or is it just the opposite — one man is able to make them better, or very few, the horse trainers, while most people, if they have to do with horses and use them, spoil them? Isn't that so, Meletus, with horses and with all other animals? Of course it is, whether you and Anytus deny it or admit it. It would be a great happiness for the young if only one man corrupted them and everyone else did them good. But the fact is, Meletus, you show plainly enough that you have never given a thought to the young. You make your own indifference clear: you have cared nothing for the things you bring me to trial over.

Tell us something more, Meletus, by Zeus: is it better to live among good citizens or bad ones? Answer, my friend; it's not a hard question. Don't bad people do some harm to those who are nearest them at any time, and good people some good?
Certainly.
Then is there anyone who would rather be harmed than helped by those he lives with? Answer, my good man; the law requires you to answer. Is there anyone who wants to be harmed?
Of course not.
Come then: do you bring me here for corrupting the young and making them worse on purpose, or without meaning to?
On purpose, I say.

What, Meletus? Are you at your age so much wiser than I am at mine? You have recognized that bad people always do some harm to those closest to them, and good people good. And have I reached such a depth of ignorance that I do not even know this: that if I make one of my companions a bad man, I run the risk of being harmed by him? And so I do this great evil on purpose, as you say? I don't believe you, Meletus, and I don't think anyone else in the world does. Either I do not corrupt them, or if I do, it is without meaning to; so that you are lying either way. And if I corrupt them without meaning to, the law is not to bring a man to court for unintended faults of that kind, but to take him aside in private and teach and warn him. For clearly, once I have learned better, I will stop doing what I do without meaning to. But you avoided my company and were unwilling to teach me, and instead you bring me here, where the law is to bring those who need punishment, not instruction.

Well, men of Athens, what I said is clear by now: Meletus has never cared about these things, much or little. But tell us all the same, Meletus: how do you say I corrupt the young? Or is it clear from the charge you wrote that it is by teaching them not to believe in the gods the city believes in, but in other, new divine things? Isn't that how you say I corrupt them, by teaching this?
That is exactly what I say.

Then by those very gods we are now speaking of, Meletus, put it still more clearly to me and to these men. I cannot make out which you mean. Do you say that I teach people to believe that there are some gods — so that I believe there are gods myself, and am not altogether godless, and do no wrong on that score — only not the gods the city believes in, but others, and that this is your charge against me, that they are others? Or do you say that I do not believe in gods at all, and teach this to others?
That is what I say: you do not believe in gods at all.
Meletus, you astonish me. Why do you say that? Don't I believe, then, that the sun and the moon are gods, as other people do?
No, by Zeus, judges — he says the sun is a stone and the moon is earth.

Do you think you are accusing Anaxagoras, my dear Meletus? Do you think so little of these men, and suppose them so unlettered, that they don't know the books of Anaxagoras of Clazomenae are full of such statements? And the young, I suppose, learn these things from me — when they can sometimes buy them in the orchestra for a drachma, at the very most, and laugh at Socrates if he pretends they are his own, especially when they are so strange. But by Zeus, is that what you think of me? That I believe in no god at all?
No, by Zeus, none whatsoever.

No one can believe you, Meletus — not even, I think, you yourself. This man, men of Athens, seems to me thoroughly insolent and reckless, and to have brought this charge out of sheer insolence, recklessness and youth. He is like a man making up a riddle to test me: Will Socrates the wise notice that I am joking and contradicting myself, or will I fool him and the rest of my hearers? For he seems to me to contradict himself in the charge, as if he said: ‘Socrates does wrong by not believing in gods, but by believing in gods.’ And that is the work of a man at play.

Look with me, gentlemen, at why he seems to me to be saying this. And you, Meletus, answer us. And you others, remember what I asked of you at the beginning, and do not make an uproar if I carry on the argument in my usual way.

Is there anyone in the world, Meletus, who believes there are human doings, but does not believe in human beings? Let him answer, gentlemen, and not make one uproar after another. Is there anyone who does not believe in horses, but believes in the doings of horses? Or who does not believe in flute players, but believes in the doings of flute players? There is not, best of men. If you won't answer, I will say it for you and for these others. But answer the next question at least: is there anyone who believes there are divine doings, but does not believe in divine beings?
There is not.

How kind of you to answer, grudgingly, when these men made you. Now, you say that I believe in divine things and teach them — new or old, no matter; at any rate I believe in divine things by your account, and you swore to that in your charge. But if I believe in divine things, then surely I must believe in divine beings too. Isn't that so? It is; I take it you agree, since you don't answer. And don't we hold that divine beings are either gods or the children of gods? Yes or no?
Certainly.

Then if I believe in divine beings, as you say, and if divine beings are gods of some kind, that would be the riddle and the joke I say you are making: that I do not believe in gods, and then again that I do believe in gods, since I believe in divine beings. And if divine beings are children of gods, bastard children by nymphs or by some other mothers, as the stories say — who in the world would believe that there are children of gods but no gods? It would be just as strange as believing in the offspring of horses and donkeys — mules — and not believing in horses and donkeys. No, Meletus, it cannot be otherwise: you brought this charge either to test us, or because you were at a loss for any real wrong to charge me with. But that you should persuade anyone with even a little sense that the same man can believe in things divine and godly, and yet believe in neither divine beings nor gods nor heroes — there is no way that can be done.

In fact, men of Athens, to show that I do no wrong under Meletus' charge does not seem to me to need much of a defense; this is enough. But what I said earlier, that I have come to be greatly hated, and by many people — be sure that it is true. And that is what will convict me, if anything does: not Meletus, and not Anytus, but the slander and envy of the many. It has convicted many other good men, and I think it will again. There is no danger that it will stop with me.

Now perhaps someone might say: Are you not ashamed, Socrates, of having followed a way of life that has put you in danger of death today? To him I would make a just reply: You are wrong, my friend, if you think that a man who is worth anything at all ought to weigh the risk of living or dying, and not look to this alone whenever he acts: whether what he does is just or unjust, the work of a good man or a bad one. By your reasoning, the demigods who died at Troy would be poor creatures, and especially the son of Thetis. He so despised danger, when the alternative was to endure disgrace, that when he was eager to kill Hector, and his mother, a goddess, spoke to him in words something like these, as I recall: My child, if you avenge the killing of your friend Patroclus and kill Hector, you yourself will die — ‘for straight after Hector,’ she says, ‘your own doom stands ready’ — he heard this and thought nothing of death and danger. He was far more afraid to live as a coward and leave his friends unavenged. ‘Let me die at once,’ he says, ‘once I have made the wrongdoer pay, so that I do not stay here, a laughingstock beside the curved ships, a burden on the earth.’ Do you suppose he gave a thought to death and danger?

For this is the truth of it, men of Athens. Wherever a man has taken up his post, believing it best, or has been posted by his commander, there, as I think, he must stay and face the danger, and take no account of death or of anything else before disgrace. So I would have done a terrible thing, men of Athens, if, when the commanders you chose to command me gave me my post at Potidaea and at Amphipolis and at Delium, I stayed where they posted me, like anyone else, and risked death; but when the god gave me my post, as I supposed and believed, with orders to live as a philosopher, examining myself and others, I then deserted it through fear of death or of anything else whatever. That would be terrible, and then indeed someone might justly bring me to court for not believing that there are gods, since I disobeyed the oracle, and feared death, and thought I was wise when I was not. For to fear death, gentlemen, is nothing other than to think oneself wise when one is not; it is to think one knows what one does not know. No one knows whether death may not be the greatest of all goods for a human being; yet people fear it as if they knew for certain that it is the greatest of evils. And is this not that shameful ignorance, the ignorance of thinking one knows what one does not know? In this too, gentlemen, I am perhaps different from most people; and if I were to claim to be wiser than anyone in anything, it would be in this: that since I do not know enough about the things in Hades, I do not think I know. But to do wrong, and to disobey one's better, whether god or man — that I do know to be evil and shameful. So I will never fear or flee from things that for all I know may be good, in preference to evils that I know to be evils.

So even if you acquit me now, and do not believe Anytus — who said that either I should never have been brought here at all, or, now that I have been, you cannot fail to put me to death, and told you that if I got off, your sons would all be practicing what Socrates teaches and would be utterly corrupted — suppose you said to me in reply: Socrates, this time we will not listen to Anytus. We acquit you, but on this condition, that you no longer spend your time in this inquiry, and give up philosophy. If you are caught still doing it, you will die. If you acquitted me, as I say, on those terms, I would say to you: Men of Athens, I have the warmest regard and love for you, but I will obey the god rather than you. As long as I draw breath and am able, I will not stop practicing philosophy, and urging you on, and making things plain to any one of you I happen to meet, saying the kind of thing I always say: Best of men, you are an Athenian, a citizen of the greatest city, the one most famous for wisdom and strength. Are you not ashamed to care about money, and how to get as much of it as you can, and about reputation and honor, while for wisdom and truth, and for your soul and how to make it as good as possible, you have no care and no thought? And if any of you disputes this, and says he does care, I will not let him go at once or leave him. I will question him, and examine him, and test him; and if he does not seem to me to possess virtue, but says he does, I will reproach him for setting the least value on the things worth most, and a higher value on things that are worth less. This I will do for anyone I meet, young or old, foreigner or citizen — but more for you citizens, since you are closer to me in blood. For this is what the god commands, be sure of it; and I believe that no greater good has ever come to you in this city than my service to the god. For I go about doing nothing else but persuading you, young and old alike, not to care for your bodies or your money before, or as much as, your soul and how to make it as good as possible. I tell you: Virtue does not come from money, but from virtue come money and every other good thing for human beings, in private life and in public. Now if I corrupt the young by saying this, then this must be harmful. But if anyone says that I say something other than this, he is talking nonsense. Therefore, men of Athens, I would say: do as Anytus tells you or not, acquit me or not, knowing that I will not act otherwise, not even if I am to die many times over.

Do not make an uproar, men of Athens. Keep to what I asked of you: not to cry out at what I say, but to listen. I believe you will be the better for listening. For I am going to tell you some other things at which you will perhaps shout; but do not do it. Be sure of this: if you put me to death, being the kind of man I say I am, you will harm yourselves more than you harm me. Meletus cannot harm me, nor can Anytus. He could not, for I do not think it is permitted that a better man be harmed by a worse. He might perhaps kill me, or drive me into exile, or strip me of my rights as a citizen. Perhaps he thinks, and others think, that these are great evils. I do not. I think it far worse to do what he is doing now, trying to put a man to death unjustly. So now, men of Athens, I am far from making this defense for my own sake, as one might suppose. I make it for yours, so that you may not, by condemning me, offend against the god's gift to you. For if you put me to death, you will not easily find another like me, a man simply — though it sounds rather comic to say it — fastened on the city by the god, as upon a great and noble horse that is somewhat sluggish because of its size and needs to be stirred up by a gadfly. That, I think, is the sort of thing the god has fastened me on the city to be: one who never stops rousing each one of you, and persuading you, and reproaching you, settling on you everywhere the whole day long. You will not easily come by another like that, gentlemen; if you take my advice, you will spare me. But perhaps you may be annoyed, like sleepers woken from a doze, and may strike out at me, and, doing as Anytus says, easily kill me; and then you would go on sleeping for the rest of your lives, unless the god in his care for you were to send you someone else. That I am the kind of man to have been given to the city by the god, you may see from this: it does not look like a merely human thing that I have neglected all my own affairs, and have put up with the neglect of my household for so many years now, while I was always busy with what is yours, going to each of you in private like a father or an elder brother, and urging you to care for virtue. If I got anything out of it, and gave this advice for pay, there would be some sense in it. But as it is, you see for yourselves that my accusers, who accused me so shamelessly of everything else, could not bring themselves to the shamelessness of producing a witness to say that I ever took a fee from anyone or asked for one. I think I produce witness enough that I am telling the truth: my poverty.

Perhaps it may seem strange that I go around giving this advice in private and meddling in other people's business, yet do not dare to come before your Assembly in public and advise the city. The reason for this is something you have often heard me speak of, in many places: something from the god, a divine thing, comes to me — the very thing Meletus made fun of in the charge he wrote. It began when I was a child: a kind of voice that comes to me, and whenever it comes it always turns me back from what I am about to do, and never urges me on. This is what opposes my taking part in politics; and I think it does very well to oppose it. For be sure of this, men of Athens: if I had tried long ago to take part in politics, I would have been dead long ago, and would have been of no use either to you or to myself. And do not be angry with me for telling the truth. No man on earth will be safe who honestly opposes you, or any other crowd, and prevents many unjust and unlawful things from being done in his city. Anyone who really fights for what is just, if he is to survive even for a short time, must live as a private man and not a public one.

I will give you strong proofs of this — not words, but what you value, deeds. Hear what happened to me, so that you may know that I would not give way to any man against what is just through fear of death, even if I should die for not giving way. What I am going to tell you is the common stuff of the law courts, but it is true. I have never held any other office in the city, men of Athens, but I did serve on the Council. And it happened that our tribe, Antiochis, was presiding when you resolved to try as a body the ten generals who had failed to pick up the men after the sea battle — unlawfully, as all of you later came to think. On that occasion I alone of the presiding members opposed your doing anything against the laws, and voted against it. The orators were ready to denounce me and have me arrested, and you were urging them on and shouting; but I thought I ought to run the risk with law and justice on my side, rather than side with you in an unjust decision out of fear of prison or death. That was while the city was still a democracy. But when the oligarchy came in, the Thirty in their turn sent for me and four others to the Rotunda, and ordered us to bring Leon of Salamis from Salamis to be put to death. They gave many such orders to many other people too, wanting to implicate as many as possible in their guilt. Then I showed once again, not in word but in deed, that I do not care a straw for death, if that is not too crude a way to put it, but that I care with all my heart about doing nothing unjust or unholy. That government, powerful as it was, did not frighten me into doing anything unjust. When we came out of the Rotunda, the other four went to Salamis and brought Leon in, but I went off home. And perhaps I would have been put to death for it, if that government had not been overthrown soon afterward. Of these things you will have many witnesses.

Do you think, then, that I would have lived so many years if I had been active in public life, and, acting as a good man should, had come to the aid of what is just, and had put that first, as one must? Far from it, men of Athens; nor would any other man. But through my whole life, in any public business I have had a part in, you will find me the same man that I am in private: one who never yet gave way to anyone in anything against what is just — neither to anyone else, nor to any of those whom my slanderers call my pupils. I have never been anyone's teacher. But if anyone, young or old, wants to hear me talking and going about my own business, I have never grudged it to him. Nor do I talk for a fee and keep silent without one; I offer myself to rich and poor alike to be questioned, and if anyone wishes, he may answer me and hear what I have to say. And whether any of these people turns out well or badly, I cannot justly be held responsible; for I never promised any of them any instruction, and never gave any. If anyone says he ever learned or heard anything from me in private that everyone else did not, be sure he is not telling the truth.

Why is it, then, that some people enjoy spending a great deal of time in my company? You have heard why, men of Athens; I told you the whole truth. They enjoy hearing the examination of those who think they are wise and are not. It is not unpleasant. But for me, as I say, this is a duty laid on me by the god, through oracles and through dreams and in every way in which any divine dispensation has ever ordered a human being to do anything. This, men of Athens, is true, and easily tested. For if I am corrupting some of the young, and have corrupted others, then surely those of them who have grown older, and have come to see that I once gave them bad advice when they were young, ought now to come up here themselves and accuse me and take their revenge. Or if they were unwilling to do it themselves, some of their families, their fathers and brothers and other relations, ought now to remember it and take revenge, if their kin suffered any harm at my hands. Many of them, certainly, are here; I can see them. First there is Crito, a man of my own age and my own deme, the father of Critobulus here. Then Lysanias of Sphettus, the father of Aeschines here. And here is Antiphon of Cephisia, the father of Epigenes. Then there are others whose brothers have spent their time in this way: Nicostratus the son of Theozotides, the brother of Theodotus — and Theodotus is dead, so he at least could not beg his brother to be silent — and Paralius here, the son of Demodocus, whose brother was Theages. And here is Adeimantus the son of Ariston, whose brother Plato is here; and Aeantodorus, whose brother Apollodorus is here. I could name many others for you, and Meletus certainly ought to have called one of them as a witness during his own speech. If he forgot then, let him call one now — I yield the floor — and let him say whether he has any such witness. But you will find it is quite the opposite, gentlemen. They are all ready to help me, the corrupter, the man who does harm to their families, as Meletus and Anytus say. Those who have been corrupted might perhaps have some reason to help me. But the uncorrupted, their relations, men already advanced in years — what other reason can they have for helping me except the right and just one, that they know Meletus is lying and I am telling the truth?

Well, gentlemen, that is about all I have to say in my defense, that and perhaps more of the same. But some one of you may be indignant when he remembers his own case: how he, standing trial on a lesser charge than this, begged and pleaded with the judges with many tears, and brought his little children up here to win as much pity as he could, and many of his relations and friends as well; while I will do none of these things, and that though I am running, as it may seem, the last and greatest danger. Perhaps, with this in mind, he may harden himself against me, and, angered by this very thing, cast his vote in anger. If any of you feels that way — I do not expect it, but if so — I think I would be speaking fairly if I said to him: My good man, I too have a family of some kind. For, in Homer's own words, I am not sprung ‘from an oak or from a rock’ but from human beings; so I have a family, and sons too, men of Athens, three of them, one already a youth and two still children. And yet I will not bring any of them up here and beg you to acquit me. Why will I do none of these things? Not out of stubbornness, men of Athens, nor out of disrespect for you. Whether I face death with confidence or not is another question. But for my good name, and yours, and the whole city's, I do not think it right for me to do any of these things, at my age and with this name of mine — true or false, it is at any rate the settled opinion that Socrates is in some way different from most people. If those of you who are thought to stand out in wisdom, or in courage, or in any other virtue, are going to behave like that, it would be a disgrace. Yet I have often seen men of that kind on trial, men thought to be of some account, doing astonishing things, as if they supposed they would suffer something terrible if they were put to death — as if they would be immortal if you did not kill them. Such men seem to me to bring shame on the city, so that a foreigner might suppose that those Athenians who stand out in virtue, whom the Athenians themselves pick out for their offices and other honors, are no better than women. You must not do such things, men of Athens, those of you who are thought to be of any account at all; and if we do them, you must not allow it. You must make this plain instead: that you will much sooner convict the man who stages these pitiful scenes and makes the city ridiculous than the man who keeps quiet.

But apart from the question of good name, gentlemen, it does not seem to me just to plead with a judge, or to be acquitted by pleading. One ought to inform him and persuade him. For the judge does not sit to hand out justice as a favor, but to judge what is just; and he has sworn an oath not to show favor to whomever he pleases, but to judge according to the laws. So we must not get you into the habit of breaking your oath, and you must not get into it; neither of us would be acting piously. Do not expect me, then, men of Athens, to behave toward you in ways that I hold to be neither honorable nor just nor holy — above all, by Zeus, when I am on trial for impiety on the charge of Meletus here. For clearly, if I were to persuade you and force you by my pleading, when you are under oath, I would be teaching you not to believe that there are gods, and in making my defense I would simply be accusing myself of not believing in them. But that is far from the truth. I do believe in them, men of Athens, as none of my accusers does. And I leave it to you and to the god to judge my case in whatever way will be best for me and for you.

divergences.older: but has other new divinities of his own
divergences.lectio: but in other, new divine things
divergences.note: Daimonia is a neuter adjective, 'divine things', not a word for gods. Keeping it loose lets the cross-examination at 27b–e work in English as it does in Greek: whoever believes in divine doings must believe in divine beings, and divine beings are gods or the children of gods.

divergences.phrase: ἃ μὴ οἶδα οὐδὲ οἴομαι εἰδέναι
divergences.older: I neither know nor think that I know.
divergences.lectio: what I do not know, I do not think I know.
divergences.note: Socrates does not say he knows nothing. He says he does not mistake his ignorance for knowledge, and that this small thing is the whole of his advantage. The edition keeps the limited claim and repeats its wording at 29b.

divergences.phrase: ἐξ ἀρετῆς χρήματα καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἀγαθὰ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἅπαντα
divergences.older: from virtue comes money and every other good of man, public as well as private
divergences.lectio: from virtue come money and every other good thing for human beings, in private life and in public
divergences.note: The Greek can also be construed 'it is virtue that makes money and everything else good for human beings', which suits a man who has just pointed to his own poverty. The edition keeps the traditional construction, which is the natural order of the words, and records the other here.
